title: MB0-02081
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, a citizen of Venezuela, is claiming protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraphs 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
This is a summary of the claimant's allegations, as they appear in his Personal Information Form (PIF).

The claimant, who was living in XXXXX, had a brother, XXXXX, who was an anti-Chavez political activist. His brother had gathered on diskette some incriminating evidence of corruption concerning the former mayor of XXXXX in XXXXX.

Feeling as though his life was threatened, XXXXX gave this diskette to the claimant before he left for Canada in 2006. In 2009, the claimant's mother was visited by a journalist who was investigating embezzlement by the former mayor of XXXXX. She told the claimant's mother that she knew that this evidence existed. The claimant's mother told the journalist to contact the claimant about this evidence. The former mayor was formally charged with XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in XXXXX 2009.

When the claimant was in Canada in XXXXX 2009, he found out that the Bolivarian Militia had entered his mother's home looking for him and XXXXX. The claimant's stepfather, who lived with his mother, was stopped on the premises and was found murdered on the public roadway. A threatening note regarding the claimant and XXXXX was found in the claimant's mother's home. She filed a complaint with the police.

On XXXXXX, 2009, the claimant returned voluntarily to Venezuela. He returned the diskettes to the journalist who had come to see his mother previously. The journalist told the claimant that the government was controlling everything but advised him to file a complaint to the office of the attorney general.

On XXXXXX, 2009, the claimant filed a complaint there. He moved from home to home with his family. He learned from lawyer friends that his name was on file in a database of people considered to be traitors by the government.
On XXXXX, 2010, the claimant left Venezuela and arrived in Canada the same day; he claimed refugee protection there.
The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity, which was established by means of the exhibits submitted on file, especially his passport.1
After reviewing the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.
The claimant is not credible.

When asked whether the claimant's brother XXXXX had been involved in political activities, the claimant responded that he had not and added that this brother worked for the XXXXXXXXXXX in the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The panel asked him again whether his brother was involved in other activities aside from his work that were related to political activities, whether social or political. Once again, the claimant said no. He added that he did not know whether his brother XXXXX was involved in other political activities.

The panel told the claimant that he had written in the second paragraph of question 31 of his PIF that his brother XXXXX was [translation] "an activist who opposed the ruling regime in Venezuela." The claimant then did an about-face and stated that his brother was part of the opposition and that he had not understood the question correctly.

The panel rejects this explanation because it is not satisfactory. The panel asked the question more than once; the question was not complex, and the claimant did not indicate that he did not understand it even though the panel had informed the claimant in its instructions at the beginning of the hearing that if he did not understand a question, he had to inform the panel. Furthermore, the claimant spontaneously responded negatively three times. In addition, the claimant does not have any intellectual and cognitive deficiencies-he is an educated person, is XXXXXXXX, and was the XXXXXXXXXXXXXX where he was responsible for XXXX employees, which indicates that his abilities are at the very least average. Rather, the panel is of the opinion that if the claimant's brother, XXXXX, had really been an anti-Chavez political activist and that if the claimant had suffered for that reason, he would not have spontaneously said no on more than one occasion, and he would not have contradicted question 31 of his PIF by stating that he did not think that his brother XXXXX was involved in anti-governmental political activism. All of this undermines his credibility significantly given that the claimant's refugee protection claim is based on his brother XXXX's anti-governmental political activism.

The claimant stated that he had been afraid of being killed since XXXXX 2009, when his mother's spouse, Mr. XXXXX, had allegedly been killed. He added that this took place on XXXXX, 2009, when an armed group went to his mother's home.

When asked what the name of this armed group was, the claimant stated that he did not know the name of this group. Then, after a moment, he stated that it was the Bolivarian Circles. When asked why he had responded that he did not know the name of this group, the claimant stated that he had understood from the question that he was being asked for the names of each person in this group.

When asked why the claimant had stated that it was the Bolivarian Circles who had gone to his mother's home and not the Bolivarian Militia, as he had written in question 31 of his PIF, the claimant stated that it was the same thing. He then added that when they are in uniform, they are called Bolivarian Militia, and when they are in civilian clothing, they are called Bolivarian Circle. Then, the claimant stated that they had been in uniform at his mother's home. He added: [translation] "I wrote Bolivarian Militia, but when I spoke, I became confused when I stated Bolivarian Circle."

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's testimony about the question of the Bolivarian Circles or Bolivarian Militia who allegedly went to the claimant's mother's home on XXXXXX, 2009, is vague, confused and contradictory. The claimant stated that he did not know the name of the group that went to his mother's home, and then he stated that it was the Bolivarian Circle, whereas in his PIF, it is written that it was the Bolivarian Militia. According to the claimant's testimony, there is a difference-one is in civilian clothing and the other is in uniform. The panel is of the opinion that if the claimant had really learned from his mother (when he was in Calgary, in Canada) that on XXXXXX, 2009, the Bolivarian Circles had gone to her home armed, threatening, and looking for the claimant and his brother XXXXX, and that if, according to his testimony, this visit had caused the claimant to be so afraid that since that day, he is afraid of being murdered, the claimant would not have contradicted himself concerning the identity of this group when he knew the difference between the two, and he also would not have stated that he did not know the name of this group. All of this undermines the claimant's credibility. The panel is of the opinion that he failed to establish that the death of his stepfather was related to the claimant's and his brother XXXXX problems.

Furthermore, the claimant stated that this Bolivarian Circles group went to his mother's home twice-on XXXXX and XXXXX, 2009. The claimant then stated that this was not correct and that the Bolivarian Circles had only gone to his mother's home once, on XXXXX, 2009. He stated that he was nervous, that it was the first time that he had testified before a panel, and that he had gotten confused.

The panel is of the opinion that this nervousness did not explain why the claimant changed his testimony. First, he stated that the Bolivarian Circles had killed his stepfather on XXXXX, 2009, when they went to the claimant's mother's home, but then he stated that they had in fact gone twice, indicating that it was during the second visit-on XXXXX, 2009-that the murder took place. He then retracted these facts and stated that it was only on XXXXX that the Bolivarian Circles had come.

In light of the analysis set out above, the panel attaches no credibility to the XXXXX, 2009, incidents. As a result, although the claimant's mother's spouse may have been killed, the panel is not of the opinion that this death was related to the claimant's and his brother XXXXX's problems.

The claimant stated that his spouse and XXX children have been hiding since XXXXX, 2010, in XXXXXX, in the state of XXXXXX, which is eight hours from the capital. When asked why the claimant had indicated on April 14, 2010, at the time he had signed his PIF, that his spouse and children lived in XXXXXXXXXXX, he responded that he had thought that he had to write their address. The panel rejects this explanation because it is not credible. The panel has trouble understanding why, in question 4, he took the time to specify the cities where each member of his family (such as brothers and parents) lives, but did not do so for the members of his immediate family. The panel is of the opinion that if the claimant's immediate family had really been living in hiding since XXXXX 2009, he would have indicated this in question 4 of his PIF, or if there had been a mistake, he would have subsequently corrected it when he sent corrections (see mail dated May 12, 2012, P-12). Once again, all of this undermines the claimant's credibility.

The claimant stated that he filed two complaints to the authorities-one on XXXXXX, 2009, in XXXXX, and the other in XXXXX 2010, in XXXXX. When asked why the claimant had written in his PIF that he had submitted only one complaint to the office of the attorney general on XXXXXX, 2009, the claimant responded that maybe at the time he had not mentioned it and that he did not know why he had not mentioned it.

When asked why the claimant stated that he had filed a complaint in XXXXXX on XXXXXX, 2009, when he had written in his PIF that on XXXXXX, 2009, he had left for XXXXX and when nothing indicated that he had then travelled towards XXXXXX before XXXXXXX, 2009, the claimant hesitated and seemed confused. When asked why the claimant had not specified that he had returned to XXXXXX between XXXXXX and XXXXXX, 2009, when he allegedly filed his first complaint, the claimant responded that maybe he had forgotten that and that maybe he had not mentioned a few details in his PIF. The claimant's counsel asked the panel to consider paragraph four of page four of question 31 of the PIF, which states that the claimant and his family had moved from one home to another and from one family to another. In the panel's opinion, this paragraph does not specify the dates or the locations of the claimant's and his family's moves. However, it is clearly specified that on XXXXXX, 2009, the claimant left for XXXXX. The panel is of the opinion that if, according to his testimony, the claimant had taken the airplane in the following days in order to go to XXXXXX to file a complaint there, he would have made the effort to specify it in his PIF.

Additionally, the claimant gave an explanation for why he did not have any corroborating document regarding the filing of his complaints in XXXXXX and in XXXXX; this explanation seemed inconsistent to the panel and is not, furthermore, corroborated by the documentary evidence. The claimant stated that when you file a complaint against a politician, there is a special division at the office of the attorney general (fiscalia) where you can only file verbal complaints, thus ensuring the confidentiality of the complaint. The claimant added, however, that the police officer who receives the complaint receives it in writing. This special division is apparently called [translation] "the victim-reporting department" or "crime news" (Noticias criminas). The claimant added that therefore, his lawyers told him that there was no corroborative evidence for his complaints given that the nature of this special division was to provide no copy or corroborating document, in order to preserve the confidentiality of the complaint.

When asked whether the claimant had thought to ask his lawyers since he had been in Canada to provide him with a document indicating that they were unable to obtain evidence for him to corroborate his police complaints, the claimant stated that he had not thought of that. Given that the claimant thought to submit to the Refugee Protection Division documents such as an article on the former mayor of XXXXXX, whom he fears, and on the murder of his stepfather, the panel is of the opinion that if the claimant had really asked his lawyers to find him corroborative evidence of his complaints and that this had not been possible, he would have thought to submit a letter from his lawyers, on the day of his hearing, explaining the steps that they had taken and why they had not found any corroborative document. The panel is also of the opinion that if the claimant had really submitted two complaints to the police, he would have thought to write this in his PIF. In addition, it seems implausible to the panel that there would be a special division within the office of the attorney general where you may file a complaint but where no document is received in order to ensure confidentiality. The panel finds nothing to corroborate this in the documentary evidence. The panel has trouble understanding what confidentiality might be protected when, furthermore, the officer receiving the complaint does so in writing, according to the claimant. All of this does not seem credible and undermines the claimant's credibility. The panel does not consider that the claimant filed a complaint with the police.

The claimant stated that he had been afraid of being murdered by XXXXXXXXX and his associates since XXXXX 2009, at which time, when he was in Canada, he allegedly learned that his stepfather had been murdered and that some members of the Bolivarian Circle had apparently entered into his mother's home, looking for him. When asked why the claimant, who was in Canada, did not take advantage of this to claim refugee protection, like three members of his family had done previously, the claimant stated that at that time, in XXXXXX 2009, he was not aware of the seriousness of the matter. He then stated that coming to speak with his brother in Canada and then returning to XXXXXX, which he did in XXXXXX 2009, could have helped him solve the problem. He then stated that maybe just filing a report would have enabled the government to do something. He added that he led a normal life in Venezuela before his problems began.

The panel is of the opinion that if the claimant had really learned that the Bolivarian Circle was looking for him aggressively by appearing with weapons and that if his stepfather had been murdered in connection to the claimant, he would have sought protection in Canada, like his brother had done previously. Furthermore, the panel does not accept the claimant's additional explanation that he wanted to return to Venezuela in order to take care of his family, because the panel does not believe that this family is living in hiding in XXXXX.
As a result, the claimant did not establish to the panel's satisfaction the alleged elements to support his fear.

At the end of the hearing, the claimant's counsel requested an extension in order to submit documents on the political activism of the former mayor of XXXXX, who is feared by the claimant, as well as a letter from the claimant's lawyer in Venezuela indicating that the claimant cannot have evidence to corroborate his complaints. In a timely manner, the panel received documents, accepted under P-8 to P-10; P-83 is a letter from a lawyer in Venezuela. The panel attaches no probative value to this document given that the agreement in the hearing room had been that an extension would be granted in order to obtain corroborative documents from the claimant's lawyers, who had informed him that it was impossible for them to obtain a copy of the reports filed by the claimant. Document P-8 does not discuss this. With respect to the other information contained in this document, the panel indicated previously that in its opinion, the claimant is not credible. Therefore, the panel does not attach probative value to this document. The panel notes in passing that this document does not contain a letterhead or address, which in itself seems contradictory; this lawyer indicated that he was available for any relevant question, but his office address or his telephone number are not indicated.
The panel reviewed documents P-94 and P-105, which are news clippings, but because it found that the claimant was not credible, these news clippings are not relevant to the panel's decision.
For these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" or "person in need of protection."

Consequently, his refugee protection claim in Canada is rejected.
